adversarial_inceptionv3.name: Adversarial InceptionV3

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with PGD adversarial training

about: InceptionV3 trained with PGD adversarial perturbations (ε=3), making it more robust to input noise. Adversarial training often yields more brain-like representations because it forces the model to rely on shape rather than texture.

aimv2.name: AIMv2
about: AIMv2 is Apple's autoregressive image model that predicts both image tokens and text tokens jointly. It combines the strengths of visual pre-training with language grounding, achieving strong performance on downstream vision tasks.

alexnet.name: AlexNet
about: AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) was the landmark deep CNN that won ImageNet 2012 and ignited the deep learning revolution. Despite its age, it remains an important baseline, and its early convolutional layers capture low-level visual features similar to those in early visual cortex.

alexnet_random.name: AlexNet (Random Weights)
about: AlexNet with random weights serves as a lower-bound baseline. Comparing trained AlexNet against this variant isolates the contribution of learning from ImageNet data versus network architecture alone.

beit.name: BEiT
about: BEiT (BERT Pre-Training of Image Transformers) applies masked token prediction to visual patches using discrete visual tokens from DALL-E. Self-supervised training on large image collections yields rich, transferable visual representations.

bit.name: BiT (Big Transfer)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification on large-scale data, then fine-tuned

about: BiT (Big Transfer, Kolesnikov et al.) pre-trains large ResNet models on very large datasets (ImageNet-21K, JFT-300M) and fine-tunes on target tasks. The key insight is that scale and careful normalization choices enable transfer learning that rivals task-specific architectures.

blip2.name: BLIP-2

info.Pre-training: Bootstrapped language-image pre-training with frozen encoders

about: BLIP-2 (Li et al., 2023) connects a powerful frozen image encoder (EVA-ViT-G) to a language model via a lightweight Q-Former module. This enables zero-shot image-text alignment, visual question answering, and image captioning without retraining either the vision or language backbone.

briaai.name: BRIA AI (RMBG)
about: BRIA AI's RMBG model is trained specifically for background removal and image matting. Its focus on foreground/background segmentation makes it an interesting model to probe for scene-boundary and object-form representations in the brain.

clip_rn101.name: CLIP (ResNet-101)
about: CLIP with a deeper ResNet-101 image encoder. The larger capacity allows it to capture richer visual features while still being grounded in natural language through contrastive training on 400 million image-text pairs.

clip_rn101_random.name: CLIP RN101 (Random Weights)
about: CLIP ResNet-101 with random weights baseline, used to isolate the effect of CLIP training from network depth and architecture.

clip_rn50.name: CLIP (ResNet-50)

info.Training Data: 400M image-text pairs from the internet (OpenAI WIT)

about: CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) jointly trains an image encoder and text encoder to align matching image-text pairs in a shared embedding space. The ResNet-50 variant uses a standard CNN backbone. CLIP representations generalize broadly because they are grounded in natural language.

clip_rn50_random.name: CLIP RN50 (Random Weights)
about: CLIP ResNet-50 with randomly initialized weights, used as a baseline to isolate the contribution of CLIP pre-training from the architecture itself.

clip_vit_b32.name: CLIP (ViT-B/32)
about: CLIP with a Vision Transformer (ViT-B/32) backbone instead of a CNN. The global attention mechanism of transformers may capture spatial relationships differently from CNNs, making this variant particularly interesting for studying higher-level visual cortex areas.

clip_vit_b32_random.name: CLIP ViT-B/32 (Random Weights)
about: CLIP ViT-B/32 with random weights, providing a baseline to assess whether CLIP's language grounding or the transformer architecture itself drives brain predictivity.

convnext.name: ConvNeXt
about: ConvNeXt (Liu et al., 2022) modernizes CNNs by borrowing design decisions from Vision Transformers—larger kernel sizes, fewer normalization layers, GELU activations, and layer-scale. It achieves transformer-level performance while remaining a pure convolutional network.

cornet_rt.name: CORnet-RT

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with recurrent temporal dynamics

about: CORnet-RT extends CORnet-S with explicit recurrent time steps that model temporal dynamics in cortical processing. It maps to V1, V2, V4, and IT cortex and incorporates feedback connections, capturing the recurrent nature of biological visual processing.

cornet_s.name: CORnet-S
about: CORnet-S (Kubilius et al., 2019) explicitly models the primate visual hierarchy (V1→V2→V4→IT) with four areas, each implemented as a residual block with recurrent connections. Its brain-constrained architecture makes it highly predictive of neural activity in ventral visual stream areas.

cornet_z.name: CORnet-Z
about: CORnet-Z is the simplest CORnet variant—a purely feedforward CNN with four layers corresponding to V1, V2, V4, and IT. It serves as a baseline for the recurrent CORnet-S and CORnet-RT models.

cross_vit.name: CrossViT
about: CrossViT (Chen et al., 2021) processes image patches at two different scales simultaneously and fuses them via cross-attention. Multi-scale token fusion helps capture both fine-grained details and global context, potentially mimicking multi-scale processing in visual cortex.

densenet121.name: DenseNet-121
about: DenseNet-121 (Huang et al., 2017) connects each layer to every subsequent layer, creating dense skip connections. These connections encourage feature reuse and allow gradients to flow more easily, enabling effective training with fewer parameters.

densenet161.name: DenseNet-161
about: DenseNet-161 is the deepest and widest DenseNet variant. Dense connectivity between all layers promotes feature reuse and gradient flow, while the increased capacity allows the model to capture richer visual representations.

densenet161_random.name: DenseNet-161 (Random Weights)
about: DenseNet-161 with random weights, used as a baseline to evaluate the contribution of dense connectivity architecture versus learned features.

densenet169.name: DenseNet-169
about: DenseNet-169 balances depth and efficiency with dense skip connections throughout its 169 layers. A middle ground between the compact DenseNet-121 and the large DenseNet-201.

densenet201.name: DenseNet-201
about: DenseNet-201 is a deeper DenseNet variant with 201 layers and dense skip connections. The larger depth and growth rate allow richer feature hierarchies to emerge.

dinov2.name: DINOv2 (ViT-B/14)
about: DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023) trains ViT via self-supervised knowledge distillation on a curated 142M image dataset (LVD-142M). Without any labels, it learns dense, semantically rich features that transfer exceptionally well—including to predicting neural activity in high-level visual areas.

dinov2_large.name: DINOv2 Large (ViT-L/14)
about: The large variant of DINOv2, with ~307M parameters and deeper transformer blocks. Increased model capacity yields even richer visual features, often leading to better predictions of neural activity in high-level visual cortex regions like FFA and PPA.

dinov2_random.name: DINOv2 (Random Weights)
about: DINOv2 architecture with random weights, providing a baseline to measure how much of DINOv2's brain predictivity comes from self-supervised training versus the ViT architecture itself.

dreamsim_vitb16.name: DreamSim (ViT-B/16)

info.Training Data: Human perceptual similarity judgments (fine-tuned from CLIP/DINO/OpenCLIP)
info.Pre-training: Perceptual similarity fine-tuning on human triplet judgments

about: DreamSim (Fu et al., 2023) fine-tunes CLIP and DINO models on human perceptual similarity judgments, aligning model representations with human perceptual experience. ViT-B/16 backbone with perceptual grounding makes it a strong model for understanding high-level visual cortex.

dreamsim_vitb32.name: DreamSim (ViT-B/32)

info.Pre-training: Perceptual similarity fine-tuning on human triplet judgments

about: DreamSim with a ViT-B/32 backbone, trained on human perceptual similarity judgments. Slightly coarser patch size than the /16 variant but similarly aligned to human perception through triplet-based fine-tuning.

efficient_net.name: EfficientNet
about: EfficientNet (Tan & Le, 2019) scales width, depth, and resolution simultaneously using a principled compound scaling method. EfficientNet-B0 achieves high accuracy with very few parameters, making it an efficient and competitive CNN baseline.

ese_vovnet.name: ESE-VoVNet
about: ESE-VoVNet uses One-Shot Aggregation (OSA) to reduce redundancy in DenseNet's dense connections, combined with Effective Squeeze-Excitation (eSE) blocks for channel recalibration. It is designed for real-time inference on detection tasks.

eva2.name: EVA-02

info.Training Data: ImageNet-21K + MIM pre-training with CLIP features
info.Pre-training: Masked Image Modeling targeting CLIP feature space

about: EVA-02 (Fang et al., 2023) pre-trains a ViT to reconstruct CLIP features from masked image patches, combining the generalization of MIM with semantic richness of CLIP supervision. It achieves strong performance across classification, detection, and segmentation benchmarks.

fbnet.name: FBNet
about: FBNet is a mobile-optimized CNN designed by Neural Architecture Search (NAS) to maximize accuracy within mobile hardware constraints. Its efficient design prioritizes inference speed over raw accuracy.

ghost_net.name: GhostNet
about: GhostNet (Han et al., 2020) generates cheap 'ghost' feature maps using linear transformations of standard convolutions, dramatically reducing computation while maintaining accuracy. Designed for mobile and edge inference.

google_vit.name: ViT-B/16 (Google)
about: The original ViT (Vision Transformer, Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) demonstrates that pure transformer architectures can outperform CNNs on image classification when pre-trained on large datasets. Patches of the image are treated as tokens, enabling global attention from the very first layer.

google_vit_random.name: ViT-B/16 (Random Weights)
about: ViT-B/16 with random weights, used as a baseline to isolate the effect of ImageNet-21K pre-training from the attention-based transformer architecture.

hrnet.name: HRNet
about: HRNet (Wang et al., 2020) maintains high-resolution feature maps throughout the entire network, running multiple parallel convolutions at different resolutions and fusing them repeatedly. Unlike most CNNs that progressively downsample, HRNet preserves spatial detail—valuable for dense prediction tasks.

inception_rn_v2.name: Inception-ResNet-V2
about: Inception-ResNet-V2 combines Inception modules (multi-scale parallel convolutions) with residual skip connections, achieving strong accuracy by leveraging both architectural motifs. Deeper and more accurate than plain Inception or ResNet alone.

inceptionv3.name: InceptionV3
about: InceptionV3 (Szegedy et al., 2016) uses factorized convolutions and auxiliary classifiers to efficiently capture multi-scale features. Its intermediate representations have been widely used in computational neuroscience as predictors of ventral stream activity.

inceptionv4.name: InceptionV4
about: InceptionV4 simplifies and unifies the Inception architecture with a more regular design. The more homogeneous architecture provides a cleaner ablation baseline compared to the hybrid Inception-ResNet variants.

kosmos2.name: Kosmos-2

info.Training Data: Grounded Image-Caption Pairs (GRIT dataset + web data)
info.Pre-training: Grounded vision-language pre-training with bounding box grounding

about: Kosmos-2 (Peng et al., 2023) extends KOSMOS-1 with grounding capabilities—it can refer and reason about objects in images using bounding box coordinates embedded directly in the language model. This spatial grounding may produce representations more aligned with retinotopic cortical processing.

mixnet.name: MixNet
about: MixNet (Tan & Le, 2019) mixes different kernel sizes within a single depthwise convolution layer, allowing each channel to operate at the most effective receptive field size. This multi-kernel approach improves accuracy with minimal parameter overhead.

mnasnet.name: MnasNet
about: MnasNet (Tan et al., 2019) uses NAS with real mobile hardware latency as the optimization objective. It optimizes the trade-off between accuracy and inference speed on actual devices, producing architecturally diverse blocks tailored for mobile deployment.

mobilenetv2.name: MobileNetV2
about: MobileNetV2 (Sandler et al., 2018) introduces inverted residual blocks with linear bottlenecks, enabling lightweight inference on mobile devices. Its depthwise separable convolutions reduce computation dramatically compared to standard convolutions.

nomic.name: Nomic Embed Vision
about: Nomic Embed Vision is an open-weights embedding model trained for high-quality visual and text alignment. It extends CLIP-style training with improved data curation, producing semantically rich image representations useful for retrieval and classification.

nomic_random.name: Nomic Embed Vision (Random Weights)
about: Nomic Embed Vision with random weights, used as a baseline to evaluate the contribution of contrastive vision-language pre-training versus the transformer architecture alone.

resnet101.name: ResNet-101
about: ResNet-101 extends ResNet-50 with 101 layers, capturing richer visual hierarchies while still benefiting from residual connections. The deeper network generally achieves higher ImageNet accuracy and can extract more complex visual features.

resnet101_imagenet1kv1.name: ResNet-101 (ImageNet-1K v1 weights)
about: ResNet-101 trained with the original ImageNet-1K recipe (v1 weights). Compared to v2 weights, this version uses a simpler training pipeline, enabling analysis of how training recipe improvements affect brain predictivity.

resnet101_random.name: ResNet-101 (Random Weights)
about: ResNet-101 with random weights, providing a baseline for the deeper ResNet architecture without any learned visual features.

resnet18.name: ResNet-18
about: ResNet-18 (He et al., 2016) is the shallowest ResNet, with 18 layers and residual skip connections that enable training without vanishing gradients. Its relatively simple hierarchy maps well to early and intermediate visual cortex areas.

resnet18_random.name: ResNet-18 (Random Weights)
about: ResNet-18 with random weights, used as a baseline to isolate the effect of ImageNet training from the residual network architecture.

resnet50.name: ResNet-50
about: ResNet-50 (He et al., 2016) uses bottleneck residual blocks with skip connections to enable training of very deep networks. With 50 layers and ~25M parameters, it is a strong, widely-used baseline whose representations have been extensively benchmarked against ventral visual stream recordings.

resnet50_places365.name: ResNet-50 (Places365)
about: ResNet-50 trained on Places365, a large dataset of 365 indoor and outdoor scene categories. Training on scenes rather than objects may yield representations more aligned with scene-selective areas like PPA.

resnet50_random.name: ResNet-50 (Random Weights)
about: ResNet-50 with random weights, the standard lower-bound baseline showing what residual architecture alone contributes before any learning from image data.

resnet50_vggface2.name: ResNet-50 (VGGFace2)
about: ResNet-50 trained for face identity recognition on VGGFace2. Face-specialized training likely yields representations strongly aligned with the Fusiform Face Area (FFA), which is selectively activated by faces.

robust_densenet161_epsilon_3.name: Robust DenseNet-161 (ε=3)
about: DenseNet-161 with strong adversarial training (ε=3). Combining dense skip connections with adversarial robustness tests whether the improved gradient flow of DenseNet architecture also benefits adversarially robust brain predictivity.

robust_mnasnet_epsilon_3.name: Robust MnasNet (ε=3)
about: MnasNet adversarially trained with ε=3. Tests whether the efficiency-focused NAS architecture can still benefit from adversarial training to improve brain alignment.

robust_mobilenetv2_epsilon_3.name: Robust MobileNetV2 (ε=3)
about: MobileNetV2 adversarially trained with ε=3. A lightweight, robust model exploring whether efficient mobile architectures can achieve brain-like representations through adversarial training.

robust_rn18_blur_strong.name: Robust ResNet-18 (Blur – Strong)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with heavy blur augmentation

about: ResNet-18 trained with heavy Gaussian blur augmentation, forcing the network to learn features at coarse spatial scales. Strong blur training may mimic the spatial frequency preferences of the magnocellular visual pathway.

robust_rn18_blur_weak.name: Robust ResNet-18 (Blur – Weak)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with mild blur augmentation

about: ResNet-18 trained with mild Gaussian blur data augmentation. Blur training encourages the model to learn lower-frequency features and reduces reliance on high-frequency texture cues, which may improve robustness and brain alignment.

robust_rn18_epsilon_003.name: Robust ResNet-18 (ε=0.003)
about: ResNet-18 adversarially trained with a very small perturbation budget (ε=0.003). Minimal adversarial training provides slight input robustness while barely affecting natural accuracy. A useful control for the effect of adversarial training intensity.

robust_rn18_epsilon_01.name: Robust ResNet-18 (ε=0.01)
about: ResNet-18 adversarially trained with ε=0.01. Research shows that adversarial training at moderate epsilon leads to more shape-biased, brain-like representations.

robust_rn18_epsilon_025.name: Robust ResNet-18 (ε=0.025)
about: ResNet-18 with ε=0.025 adversarial training. At this epsilon, the model must learn more shape-based features rather than relying on texture statistics, potentially improving alignment with ventral visual stream.

robust_rn18_epsilon_3.name: Robust ResNet-18 (ε=3)
about: ResNet-18 with strong adversarial training (ε=3). At large epsilon, the model learns highly robust but stylized features. Research (Feather et al., 2019; Engstrom et al., 2019) shows such models correlate strongly with higher visual cortex areas.

robust_rn18_epsilon_5.name: Robust ResNet-18 (ε=5)
about: ResNet-18 with the strongest adversarial training (ε=5). Very large perturbation budgets may degrade natural task accuracy while maximizing input robustness, creating extremely shape-biased representations.

robust_rn50_blur_strong.name: Robust ResNet-50 (Blur – Strong)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with heavy blur augmentation

about: ResNet-50 trained with heavy blur augmentation, maximally de-emphasizing high-frequency texture cues and encouraging coarse spatial feature learning.

robust_rn50_blur_weak.name: Robust ResNet-50 (Blur – Weak)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with mild blur augmentation

about: ResNet-50 trained with mild Gaussian blur augmentation, encouraging lower-frequency feature learning while preserving most natural accuracy.

robust_rn50_epsilon_003.name: Robust ResNet-50 (ε=0.003)
about: ResNet-50 with very weak adversarial training (ε=0.003), a near-standard model providing a control for the effect of minimal adversarial regularization.

robust_rn50_epsilon_01.name: Robust ResNet-50 (ε=0.01)
about: ResNet-50 with moderate adversarial training (ε=0.01). This epsilon level is often where the trade-off between robustness and natural accuracy begins to significantly improve brain alignment.

robust_rn50_epsilon_025.name: Robust ResNet-50 (ε=0.025)
about: ResNet-50 adversarially trained with ε=0.025. Shape-bias increases at this epsilon, and the model's internal representations often show improved alignment with ventral stream recordings.

robust_rn50_epsilon_3.name: Robust ResNet-50 (ε=3)
about: ResNet-50 with strong adversarial training (ε=3). Engstrom et al. (2019) showed that such robustly-trained models are among the best brain predictors, suggesting that adversarial robustness and neural alignment share common computational principles.

robust_rn50_epsilon_5.name: Robust ResNet-50 (ε=5)
about: ResNet-50 with maximum adversarial training (ε=5). Pushes the model toward highly abstracted, shape-biased representations at the cost of some natural accuracy.

robust_vgg16_blur_strong.name: Robust VGG-16 (Blur – Strong)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with heavy blur augmentation

about: VGG-16 trained with heavy blur augmentation, strongly reducing reliance on high-frequency texture cues and focusing the model on coarser spatial structure.

robust_vgg16_blur_weak.name: Robust VGG-16 (Blur – Weak)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with mild blur augmentation

about: VGG-16 trained with mild blur augmentation, reducing texture bias while preserving most of the original accuracy.

robust_vgg16_bn_epsilon_3.name: Robust VGG-16 BN (ε=3)
about: VGG-16 with batch normalization adversarially trained with ε=3. The simple stacked-convolution architecture of VGG with adversarial training tests whether classic architectures can match modern models in brain alignment when robustness is enforced.

robust_vgg19_blur_strong.name: Robust VGG-19 (Blur – Strong)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with heavy blur augmentation

about: VGG-19 with heavy blur augmentation, maximizing coarse spatial feature learning in the deeper VGG architecture.

robust_vgg19_blur_weak.name: Robust VGG-19 (Blur – Weak)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with mild blur augmentation

about: VGG-19 trained with mild blur augmentation, testing whether the deeper VGG-19 architecture benefits similarly from low-frequency emphasis as VGG-16.

robust_wideresnet50_epsilon_003.name: Robust WideResNet-50 (ε=0.003)
about: WideResNet-50 with minimal adversarial training (ε=0.003). Tests whether width combined with minimal robustness training changes brain predictivity compared to standard WideResNet-50.

robust_wideresnet50_epsilon_01.name: Robust WideResNet-50 (ε=0.01)
about: WideResNet-50 with mild adversarial training (ε=0.01), beginning to improve shape-bias and brain alignment.

robust_wideresnet50_epsilon_025.name: Robust WideResNet-50 (ε=0.025)
about: WideResNet-50 with ε=0.025 adversarial training. This epsilon often represents a sweet spot between robustness and natural accuracy.

robust_wideresnet50_epsilon_3.name: Robust WideResNet-50 (ε=3)
about: WideResNet-50 with strong adversarial training (ε=3). The wide architecture combined with strong adversarial regularization may yield among the most brain-like CNN representations.

robust_wideresnet50_epsilon_5.name: Robust WideResNet-50 (ε=5)
about: WideResNet-50 with the largest adversarial perturbation budget (ε=5). Maximum robustness constraint on a wide, deep network.

siglip.name: SigLIP
about: SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) replaces CLIP's softmax contrastive loss with a sigmoid loss, enabling efficient training without large batch sizes. Trained on WebLI (web-scraped image-language pairs), it achieves strong zero-shot performance and rich semantic representations.

siglip2.name: SigLIP 2
about: SigLIP 2 improves upon the original SigLIP with better data curation, training recipes, and architecture refinements. Enhanced vision-language alignment may produce representations even more predictive of high-level visual cortex.

taskonomy_autoencoding.name: Taskonomy – Autoencoding
about: Taskonomy Autoencoding trains a ResNet encoder to reconstruct its own input, learning to preserve all spatial information. Unlike classification models, the encoder has no label pressure—only reconstruction fidelity. This task probes what low-level features are needed for pixel reconstruction.

taskonomy_class_object.name: Taskonomy – Object Classification
about: Taskonomy Object Classification trains an encoder for recognizing object categories within indoor scenes. This semantic task drives the network to learn object-level features, making it a useful comparison to general ImageNet models.

taskonomy_class_scene.name: Taskonomy – Scene Classification
about: Taskonomy Scene Classification trains an encoder to recognize indoor scene categories. Scene-level training may produce representations especially aligned with scene-selective cortex (PPA).

taskonomy_curvature.name: Taskonomy – Surface Curvature
about: Taskonomy Curvature trains an encoder to predict the curvature of surfaces in indoor scenes. This geometry-sensitive task forces the network to represent 3D shape properties rather than texture or color.

taskonomy_denoising.name: Taskonomy – Image Denoising
about: Taskonomy Denoising trains an encoder-decoder to remove synthetic noise from images. The task drives learning of spatial structure and texture statistics without any semantic labels.

taskonomy_depth_euclidean.name: Taskonomy – Depth (Euclidean)
about: Taskonomy Depth Euclidean estimates the absolute 3D distance from the camera to each surface point. Depth-sensitive representations may align with dorsal stream areas that support spatial navigation and object manipulation.

taskonomy_depth_zbuffer.name: Taskonomy – Depth (Z-buffer)
about: Taskonomy Depth Z-buffer estimates depth in the camera-aligned z-buffer format. Compared to Euclidean depth, z-buffer depth is measured perpendicular to the camera plane, capturing different geometric cues.

taskonomy_edge_occlusion.name: Taskonomy – Occlusion Edges
about: Taskonomy Occlusion Edges detects the boundaries where one surface occludes another—a geometric signal that corresponds to object outlines. This captures figure-ground separation relevant to early visual processing.

taskonomy_edge_texture.name: Taskonomy – Texture Edges
about: Taskonomy Texture Edges detects boundaries defined by texture changes rather than depth discontinuities. Texture-based edge detection captures mid-level visual features that may correlate with V2/V4 processing.

taskonomy_inpainting.name: Taskonomy – Image Inpainting
about: Taskonomy Inpainting trains an encoder-decoder to predict missing image regions given context. This requires understanding scene statistics and object structure, driving the encoder to learn rich scene-level representations.

taskonomy_keypoints2d.name: Taskonomy – 2D Keypoints
about: Taskonomy 2D Keypoints detects distinctive 2D image points (corners, junctions, salient points). This low-level feature detection task drives sensitivity to image structure without semantic labeling.

taskonomy_keypoints3d.name: Taskonomy – 3D Keypoints
about: Taskonomy 3D Keypoints detects 3D structural keypoints in indoor scenes, capturing geometric salient points in depth-aware coordinates. This extends 2D keypoint detection to three dimensions.

taskonomy_normal.name: Taskonomy – Surface Normals
about: Taskonomy Surface Normals predicts the orientation of surfaces at each pixel—a geometric task that requires understanding 3D shape. This is a rich signal for scene geometry understanding related to spatial processing in dorsal cortex.

taskonomy_reshading.name: Taskonomy – Reshading
about: Taskonomy Reshading trains the network to predict how a scene should look under different illumination conditions. Intrinsic image decomposition into shading requires understanding 3D geometry and material properties.

taskonomy_segment_semantic.name: Taskonomy – Semantic Segmentation
about: Taskonomy Semantic Segmentation assigns a semantic category label to every pixel. This drives the encoder to learn high-level object and region representations, potentially aligning with category-selective cortical areas.

taskonomy_segment_unsup25d.name: Taskonomy – Unsupervised Segmentation (2.5D)
about: Taskonomy Unsupervised 2.5D Segmentation groups pixels based on depth discontinuities and appearance, without semantic labels. The 2.5D signal integrates 2D appearance with depth cues.

taskonomy_segment_unsup2d.name: Taskonomy – Unsupervised Segmentation (2D)
about: Taskonomy Unsupervised 2D Segmentation groups pixels purely by visual similarity without depth or semantic information. This purely appearance-driven task is a mid-level vision signal without category or 3D supervision.

tdann_simclr.name: TDANN (SimCLR)
about: TDANN (Topographic Deep Artificial Neural Network) adds a spatial smoothness constraint on top of SimCLR self-supervised training to model the topographic organization of visual cortex. Units that are spatially nearby in the network learn to prefer similar stimuli, mimicking the cortical layout.

tdann_simclr_alpha_10.name: TDANN (SimCLR, α=10)
about: TDANN with topographic loss weight α=10, applying strong spatial organization pressure. Higher α encourages stronger cortical-like topographic maps, potentially improving voxel-by-voxel brain predictivity.

tdann_simclr_alpha_100.name: TDANN (SimCLR, α=100)
about: TDANN with the strongest topographic loss weight α=100. Maximum spatial organization constraint; may sacrifice task accuracy to achieve highly regular topographic structure.

tdann_simclr_alpha_2.name: TDANN (SimCLR, α=2)
about: TDANN with topographic loss weight α=2. Lower α means weaker spatial organization pressure, allowing more flexibility in learned features while still encouraging some topographic structure.

tdann_simclr_alpha_5.name: TDANN (SimCLR, α=5)
about: TDANN with topographic loss weight α=5, providing moderate spatial organization pressure. This intermediate setting balances brain-inspired topographic structure with task performance.

toponets_rn18.name: TopoNet (ResNet-18)
about: TopoNets apply a topographic organization loss on top of supervised training, enforcing spatial smoothness analogous to how orientation preference maps appear in visual cortex. The ResNet-18 backbone keeps the model compact while the topographic constraint improves brain alignment.

toponets_rn18_tau_0.5.name: TopoNet RN18 (τ=0.5)
about: TopoNet ResNet-18 with τ=0.5, the strongest locality constraint (sharp Gaussian smoothing). This setting enforces fine-grained topographic structure, most closely mimicking the local preference maps seen in cortex.

toponets_rn18_tau_1.name: TopoNet RN18 (τ=1)
about: TopoNet ResNet-18 with τ=1. A moderate-strength topographic constraint that enforces spatial smoothness over a slightly wider neighborhood than τ=0.5.

toponets_rn18_tau_20.name: TopoNet RN18 (τ=20)
about: TopoNet ResNet-18 with τ=20. Very weak topographic constraint; the model is close to standard supervised training with minimal cortical topography imposed.

toponets_rn18_tau_5.name: TopoNet RN18 (τ=5)
about: TopoNet ResNet-18 with τ=5. A weaker topographic constraint, enforcing broad spatial smoothness over large neighborhoods.

toponets_rn18_tau_50.name: TopoNet RN18 (τ=50)
about: TopoNet ResNet-18 with τ=50. The weakest topographic constraint in the τ sweep, essentially functioning as supervised ResNet-18 with minimal spatial organization pressure.

toponets_rn50.name: TopoNet (ResNet-50)
about: TopoNet with the larger ResNet-50 backbone, applying topographic organization constraints during supervised training. The larger capacity combined with brain-inspired topographic structure aims to improve predictions across multiple visual ROIs.

toponets_vit.name: TopoNet (ViT)

info.Pre-training: Supervised + Topographic organization constraint on ViT

about: TopoNet with a Vision Transformer backbone, applying topographic organization constraints to attention-based features. Combining transformer global attention with cortical topographic structure is a novel approach to brain-inspired visual modeling.

vgg16_imagenet1kv1.name: VGG-16
about: VGG-16 (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) uses a simple but effective architecture of 3×3 convolutions stacked in increasing depth. Its straightforward hierarchy has been extensively used in computational neuroscience as a predictor of ventral stream representations.

vgg16_imagenet1kv1_random.name: VGG-16 (Random Weights)
about: VGG-16 with random weights, used as a baseline to measure the contribution of ImageNet training versus the stacked convolutional architecture alone.

vgg19_imagenet1kv1.name: VGG-19
about: VGG-19 extends VGG-16 with three additional convolutional layers, increasing depth and representational capacity. The larger hierarchy can capture more complex visual features across the ventral visual stream.

vgg19_imagenet1kv1_random.name: VGG-19 (Random Weights)
about: VGG-19 with random weights, a baseline for isolating the contribution of ImageNet training from the deep convolutional architecture.

vone_alexnet.name: VOneNet (AlexNet)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with fixed V1 Gabor front-end

about: VOneNet AlexNet (Dapello et al., 2020) replaces the first convolutional layer with a fixed bank of Gabor filters that model V1 simple cells, complete with noise injection. This biologically-constrained front-end improves robustness to adversarial perturbations and distortions.

vone_cornet_s.name: VOneNet (CORnet-S)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with fixed V1 Gabor front-end

about: VOneNet CORnet-S combines the V1-like Gabor front-end from VOneNet with the brain-constrained recurrent architecture of CORnet-S. This combination aims to simultaneously model both V1 processing and the recurrent dynamics of higher visual areas.

vone_rn50.name: VOneNet (ResNet-50)

info.Pre-training: Supervised classification with fixed V1 Gabor front-end

about: VOneNet ResNet-50 uses a ResNet-50 backbone with a biologically-constrained V1 front-end (fixed Gabor filters + noise). The combination of a strong ImageNet-trained backbone with a brain-inspired first stage produces robust, brain-like visual representations.

webssl_dino300m.name: WebSSL DINO (300M)

info.Pre-training: DINO self-supervised distillation at web scale

about: WebSSL DINO 300M scales DINO self-supervised training to 300M parameters trained on 3 billion web images. Web-scale training without curated datasets tests whether sheer data and model scale alone can match curated pipelines for predicting brain activity.

webssl_mae300m.name: WebSSL MAE (300M)
about: WebSSL MAE 300M scales Masked Autoencoding (He et al., 2022) to 300M parameters on 3 billion web images. MAE trains a ViT encoder to reconstruct masked patches, and at web scale it tests how reconstruction-based self-supervision compares to distillation-based approaches for brain predictivity.

wideresnet101.name: WideResNet-101
about: WideResNet-101 combines increased depth (101 layers) with increased width, providing the largest standard WideResNet in this benchmark. Its combination of depth and width gives it among the richest feature hierarchies in the CNN family.

wideresnet50.name: WideResNet-50
about: WideResNet-50 (Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2016) trades depth for width, doubling the number of channels in each residual block. Wider networks can sometimes achieve higher accuracy than deeper networks, and broader filters may capture different visual features than deep narrow networks.

xception.name: Xception
about: Xception (Chollet, 2017) replaces Inception modules with depthwise separable convolutions, which fully decouple spatial feature learning from channel mixing. This extreme version of Inception achieves better accuracy than Inception-V3 with similar parameter count.
